title: dreaming of a cocoon
content:
recently, my mother found a caterpillar eating its way through her houseplant. we debated about letting it outside — would it die in the winter cold, if it had been born in our living room? I decided to try my best to take care of the caterpillar — in hopes it would become a cocoon, and maybe, one day, a butterfly.

I moved it into a new home — a plastic bowl, then a large mason jar. I gave it food, and twigs to climb on. I checked on it multiple times a day, for signs that it was about to pupate and turn itself into a cocoon, where it then lay dormant for weeks, or months, inside its caterpillar soup.

I was very excited to witness this process. I’ve been going through a difficult, liminal time (documented in my sketchbooks here + here) and I felt comforted by a tiny creature who was doing what it needed to do to get through winter. it felt like a gift from life — to be offered an opportunity to witness metamorphosis, when my own life felt so uncertain.

but… after a few days, my caterpillar died.

I could feel guilty and blame myself — maybe I moved it too many times, maybe it needed to hang there longer, maybe I should’ve just let it free, maybe I disturbed it too much — but, when I saw its unmoving body, I just felt a tiny terror and grief over this caterpillar — grief that I know is displaced attachment grief, from missing Luna, my Istanbul life, my home.


I wanted to cocoon together. but I guess I will cocoon alone, which is fine. I know how to cocoon. I make worlds like cocoons.

I’m grateful to be reminded of what I need during this time. I need the fertile incubation period of stillness, silence, rest. I need to allow hibernation, and death, and rebirth, and all the soupy metabolizing that happen in between. this is ultimately about trusting in process — even if it feels dark and terrifying. one day, we’ll emerge from this.
